opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the more important questions for how things go, and my view is roughly that it's quite plausible we lose the property that models mostly reason in natural language, but it's not guaranteed, and the timing really matters.

Right now we're in a somewhat lucky situation. The models are transformers with a fairly limited amount of serial computation per forward pass. If they want to do a lot of serial reasoning, like working through a hard math problem or planning several steps ahead, they basically have to write it out as tokens. That chain of thought is in English, or something close to it, and we can read it. It's not perfectly faithful, and there are real issues with models not saying everything that's driving their behavior, but it's a pretty big affordance for safety. If a model is scheming in some sophisticated way that requires a lot of thinking, there's a decent chance some of that shows up in the text.

The question is whether people will move to architectures where the model can do a lot of serial reasoning in its internal states, what people sometimes call "neuralese": recurrence, passing high-dimensional vectors forward instead of discrete tokens, continuous latent chain of thought, that kind of thing. There have been research papers on this, and there are obvious reasons it might be more efficient. A token is a pretty narrow bottleneck. You're compressing this huge activation vector down to one of maybe a hundred thousand options at every step, and that throws away a lot of information. So naively you'd expect reasoning in latent space to be more expressive.

But in practice, so far, these approaches haven't clearly beaten just doing reinforcement learning on natural-language chain of thought. A few reasons I think that's been true. One, there's a huge amount of pretraining data in natural language, and the model's ability to reason in words piggybacks on all of that. Neuralese starts from scratch in some sense. Two, training recurrent or latent-reasoning architectures is often harder. You lose some of the parallelism that makes transformers so efficient to train, and credit assignment through long latent chains can be tricky. Three, the current paradigm is working really well, so there's less pressure to switch.

So my guess is something like: in the near term, the next couple of years, it's more likely than not that frontier models still do most of their heavy reasoning in something like legible text. But over a longer horizon, especially once AIs are doing a lot of the AI research themselves and can search over architectures much more aggressively, I'd put substantial probability on someone finding a way to make latent reasoning work better, and then competitive pressure pushes everyone toward it. If it's, say, a meaningful efficiency gain, I don't expect labs to forgo that purely for safety reasons, unless there's coordination or regulation, or unless the safety case is really clearly articulated.

There's also an intermediate world worth worrying about, where the text is still there but drifts away from being meaningful English. If you do a lot of RL on outcomes, the chain of thought can get compressed, weird, or steganographic, even without an architecture change. So even preserving the token bottleneck doesn't fully guarantee legibility.

From a safety perspective, I think a few things follow. It's worth labs explicitly valuing legible reasoning and being willing to pay some cost for it. It's worth not training directly against the chain of thought in ways that teach models to hide things. And we should be using this period where reasoning is legible to learn as much as we can, and to build control and monitoring techniques that don't totally depend on it, because I don't think we should bank on it lasting.

r002.rationale: It describes recurrence and latent reasoning as ways models could perform serial reasoning in internal states rather than writing it out as tokens.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that this is an area that's actively being pushed on, and I'd put substantial probability on it happening — like, maybe 30 or 40% that within a few years the frontier models are doing a meaningful amount of their serial reasoning in some latent form rather than in tokens. But I want to be careful to distinguish between a few different things people mean here, because they have pretty different implications.

One version is what you might call recurrence or latent chain of thought — you let the model pass its residual stream, or some continuous vector, back into itself for many steps instead of forcing it to sample a token at each step. There have been research results on this, and they do show gains on some tasks. But the thing I'd flag is that so far, the results have mostly been at small scale, and they haven't obviously beaten just doing normal chain of thought with a similar compute budget. And there's a reason to think that might persist: the discrete token bottleneck is actually a kind of regularizer, and more importantly, it's what lets you do RL on the reasoning. If you want to train the model on long reasoning traces with outcome-based rewards, having the intermediate steps be discrete tokens that the model itself can read and condition on turns out to be quite convenient. Continuous reasoning tends to be harder to optimize, you get instability, and you lose the ability to just pretrain on vast amounts of human reasoning that's already expressed in words.

So my honest view is that there's a sort of structural reason why text-based reasoning has won so far, which is that the training signal is much more available for it, not just that nobody's tried the alternative.

That said, there's a second version which I think is more likely and more concerning from a safety perspective, which is the reasoning stays in tokens but the tokens stop meaning what they appear to mean. So you do a huge amount of RL on outcomes, and the chain of thought drifts — it becomes steganographic, or just compressed into something that's only partially legible, with a lot of the real work happening in the forward passes between tokens anyway. You don't need any architectural change for that. You just need a lot of optimization pressure and no pressure to keep the reasoning faithful. And I think we're already seeing hints of this in the sense that reasoning traces from heavily RL'd models can be pretty weird and hard to read.

And then a third thing is just raw forward pass capability. As models get bigger and get more layers, more and more reasoning happens in a single forward pass that would previously have required explicit steps. That's not really an architecture change either, it's just scaling, but the effect on interpretability of the reasoning is similar.

So if you ask me "will the architecture change in a way that removes textual reasoning," I'd say somewhat unlikely in the near term, maybe a quarter of the probability, mostly because the economic incentives currently favor the thing that's easy to train. But if you ask "will we end up in a world where the stuff we can read is not where the important reasoning is happening," I think that's substantially more likely, because there are three or four paths to it, and only one of them requires anyone to deliberately change the architecture.

The thing I'd really want is for labs to treat chain-of-thought legibility as something they're actively preserving — measuring whether the reasoning is faithful, not training directly against the chain of thought in ways that push it to be unreadable, and being willing to pay some capability tax to keep it. Because I think the window where we have this somewhat-legible reasoning is kind of a gift, and it's one of the main things that makes me more optimistic about catching misaligned behavior in the current generation of systems. It would be a shame to lose it through inattention rather than through some deliberate tradeoff.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s pretty plausible that you can get this to work. The basic idea would be to let the model do additional computation without requiring every intermediate step to correspond to a token that’s a word or part of a word. You could have something like a recurrent state that the model updates a bunch of times before producing its answer.

The thing I’m less sure about is how much of an advantage this gives you over reasoning in words. Language is already a pretty flexible medium for doing reasoning, and models have a lot of training data that teaches them how to use it. If you want them to reason in some other internal representation, you need a training process that actually incentivises useful computation in that representation. Just adding the capacity doesn’t necessarily get you there.

But I wouldn’t be very confident that this is a fundamental obstacle. You could imagine training on tasks where you can check the final answer, and then letting reinforcement learning find useful ways to use those intermediate computational steps. There might be substantial efficiency gains, especially for things that are awkward to express in language.

From a safety perspective, I think the important implication is that we shouldn’t assume we’ll always get a readable chain of thought. Even when the model reasons in words, those words aren’t guaranteed to faithfully explain what it’s doing. But if more of the reasoning happens in a latent state, then monitoring the verbal reasoning becomes an even less complete picture.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s quite plausible that you can get substantial gains from doing more computation that isn’t expressed in words. But I’d distinguish that from needing a fundamentally different architecture. A transformer already does a lot of computation internally that we don’t see in its output. The question is whether you can give it additional steps of computation, and train it to use those steps effectively, without requiring it to produce a human-readable chain of thought.

One approach would be to let the model pass continuous internal representations from one step to the next, rather than forcing everything through a sampled token. That potentially lets it communicate much more information between steps. But there’s a training problem: with ordinary text, you have lots of examples of useful intermediate reasoning. For these internal representations, you don’t have that supervision, so you need some other way to discover effective computations, perhaps through reinforcement learning.

So I’d be pretty uncertain about how quickly this works and how large the gains are. I wouldn’t assume that verbal reasoning is the most efficient way for these systems to think. And from a safety perspective, I wouldn’t want to rely on their reasoning remaining readable just because that’s how current systems often work.

r002.rationale: It says substantial gains are plausible, but explicitly distinguishes those gains from needing a fundamentally different architecture; it does not suggest substantial architectural changes.

r003.rationale: It does not assess papers or characterize their gains as modest.

r004.rationale: It does not say this research was underexplored because easier improvement opportunities were available elsewhere.
